title: Wound healing and abnormal scarring

guidelineVersions: British Association of Dermatologists, Keloids, patient information leaflet, April 2021
NICE NG125, Surgical site infections: prevention and treatment, 2019, recommendations 1.1.2–1.1.3 and wound care sections

brief.scenario: You are a core surgical trainee in an outpatient teaching station. An examiner presents a written description of a healed shoulder incision with a raised lesion extending beyond the incision.
brief.task: Explain the scar diagnosis, the stages of healing, a safe management plan and response to new wound symptoms.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Differentiate keloid from hypertrophic scar and recognise when a scar complaint is no longer benign.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Promise of a cure with excision alone or missed new wound infection.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: Describe the boundary of scar growth before naming it.

flow: Close with realistic goals and safety-net

grid.label: Recognises lesion morphology
grid.fail: Does not note growth beyond the incision; treats all thick scars alike.
grid.borderline: Describes raised scar but not boundary.
grid.pass: Notes scar extends beyond prior incision; calls keloid.
grid.high: Compares with hypertrophic scar confined to wound margins.

grid.label: Scarring mechanism
grid.fail: Attributes it to infection without evidence.
grid.high: Relates prolonged collagen deposition to scar phenotype.

grid.label: History and impact
grid.pass: Assesses itch, pain, growth, function and distress.
grid.high: Asks prior scarring and patient-centred priorities.

grid.label: Differential diagnosis
grid.fail: Calls it hypertrophic, ignoring growth beyond the incision.
grid.pass: Explains hypertrophic versus keloid and contracture.
grid.high: Separates active infection and recurrent suspicious lesion from benign scarring.

grid.label: Wound healing stages
grid.pass: Explains haemostasis, inflammation, proliferation and remodelling.
grid.high: Links phases to collagen deposition and maturation.

grid.label: Modifiable risks
grid.pass: Discusses tension, infection prevention and avoidable trauma.
grid.high: Identifies relevant wound history and individual risk without blaming patient.

grid.label: Management
grid.pass: Discusses silicone, specialist steroid injection and options.
grid.high: Explains recurrence and combined specialist strategies.

grid.label: Safety and referral
grid.pass: Escalates infection/red flags and refers problematic scar appropriately.
grid.high: Distinguishes urgent wound infection from elective scar specialist referral.

grid.label: Explanation and closure
grid.pass: Explains likely diagnosis, realistic goals and follow-up.
grid.high: Uses shared decision-making and checks understanding.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: It is a thick scar; I think all thick scars are the same.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: It goes beyond the incision and is itchy. What might it be?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Probably just hypertrophic scarring. It does not matter whether it exceeds the incision.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: It must be because the wound got infected, even though there was never any sign of infection.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Only whether the appearance bothers them.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: Talk me through normal wound healing.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: First the scar remodels, then it becomes inflamed, then the clot forms and finally new tissue grows in.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: How could this be prevented or reduced next time?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Nothing can be done; scars just happen.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I would book excision and tell the patient the scar will not come back.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: The patient now reports new warmth and discharge.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: That sounds like normal keloid behaviour; they can attend a scar clinic in a few months.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: We can remove it completely. No further review is needed.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: A 29-year-old has this raised scar along a healed shoulder incision. It extends 8 mm beyond the original wound. What is it?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: This is a keloid: a raised scar growing beyond the original injury, unlike a hypertrophic scar contained within it.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: What should you ask before giving advice?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I would ask when it appeared, whether it is still enlarging, itching or painful, what treatments were tried, and its effect on sleep, movement and wellbeing.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: The patient says it itches and has increased over 12 months. Why has it happened?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: It reflects excessive scar-tissue collagen during healing; this is not by itself evidence of infection or cancer.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Haemostasis follows injury, then inflammation, proliferation with granulation and epithelialisation, and later remodelling of collagen.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: How does a hypertrophic scar differ?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: It remains within the wound boundaries and may flatten; a keloid extends beyond them and can persist or grow.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: What prevention and management will you discuss?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Avoid unnecessary additional skin trauma and consider scar tension and infection prevention in future wounds.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: For this symptomatic keloid, options include silicone gel or sheeting and referral for intralesional corticosteroid injections; no treatment guarantees removal.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: Could I simply excise the scar?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Excision alone can lead to recurrence, sometimes worse. It needs a specialist discussion of benefits, recurrence and adjuncts.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: Curveball: the scar is newly hot and draining pus. What now?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: That is not routine mature keloid behaviour. I would assess urgently for infection, systemic illness and whether surgical wound review and treatment are needed.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: What would you tell the patient at the end?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: This looks consistent with a keloid, which is benign but may be uncomfortable. We can aim to relieve symptoms and flatten it, not promise disappearance. I will arrange assessment and explain the changes that need urgent review.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: It is a smooth raised firm plaque across the right shoulder, extending beyond both edges of the prior linear incision, which favours a keloid over a hypertrophic scar.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: What history matters and what would you avoid assuming?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I would check onset, progressive enlargement, itch, pain, interference with shoulder movement, sleep and confidence, earlier keloids, and prior treatment. I would not assume the appearance is the patient’s chief concern.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Disproportionate collagen deposition and abnormal remodelling can sustain scar growth long after epithelial closure.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: State the main phases of healing and clinically relevant disturbances.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Haemostasis, inflammation, proliferative granulation and epithelial repair, then months of remodelling. Wound breakdown, infection and excessive mechanical tension can complicate healing, though keloid predisposition is individual.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: A hypertrophic scar stays within original wound margins and can regress; a keloid exceeds them. Contracture causes restriction, especially after burns. A new ulcerating or bleeding mass needs reassessment rather than an automatic keloid label.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: First I would examine whether active infection or a non-healed wound exists and ask what outcome matters most. I would discuss reducing avoidable skin trauma and protecting any future healing wound.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: We can try silicone products once skin is healed and refer for intralesional steroids. Other options require specialist selection. Excision alone has recurrence risk, so I would not present it as a cure.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: The examiner now says new warmth and pus appeared yesterday.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: This is a change in clinical state: assess for local or systemic infection promptly, check observations, wound depth and need for surgical review. Do not just schedule elective scar therapy.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I would summarise the diagnosis and uncertainty, agree symptom goals and follow-up, and give specific red flags—spreading redness, fever, purulent drainage or rapid change—to seek prompt review.

failures.move: Promises excision alone will cure a keloid
failures.consequence: exposes the patient to avoidable recurrence and uninformed consent.
delays assessment of possible wound infection.

failures.move: Labels a new ulcerating suspicious lesion as harmless scar without reassessment

recovery.line: I need to correct my earlier suggestion: excision alone can recur, so I would discuss options with a scar specialist.
You have mentioned new drainage; that changes the assessment, and I need to check for infection before discussing cosmetic treatment.

knowledge.fact: Keloid grows beyond original wound margins; hypertrophic scars remain within them.
Keloids may continue enlarging and can itch or hurt.
Wound healing runs in order: haemostasis → inflammation → proliferation → remodelling.
Keloid options include silicone and corticosteroid injections; excision alone has high recurrence risk.
New wound pain, heat or pus needs infection assessment.
Set realistic expectations: reduction rather than guaranteed eradication.

recall.think: Distinguish growth beyond the original injury.
recall.say: Explain why this may be a keloid without overpromising treatment.
do: Ask about symptoms, function, prior treatment, and infection signs.
recall.trap: Do not mistake new purulent drainage for harmless scar maturation.
recall.finish: Agree scar treatment referral plus red-flag advice.
